subject: Computer Networking
title: The Smartphone Revolution
description: A 60-second lesson on The Smartphone Revolution.

hook.text: In 2007, the iPhone put a full web browser in everyone's pocket. Mobile internet usage exploded.

buildup.text: Before smartphones, mobile internet meant tiny WAP pages on flip phones. The experience was painful.

discovery.text: 3G and later 4G networks gave phones enough bandwidth for real websites, video, and app stores.

twist.text: By 2016, mobile traffic surpassed desktop traffic globally. The phone became most people's primary computer.

climax.text: App ecosystems created entirely new industries: ride-sharing, mobile payments, instant messaging at global scale.

punchline.text: The smartphone made the internet portable, personal, and constant.

quiz.question: When did global mobile internet traffic surpass desktop traffic?

details.summary: The iPhone's launch in 2007 and the subsequent smartphone revolution moved internet access from desks to pockets. Mobile internet usage surpassed desktop by 2016. Smartphones created a permanently connected population and spawned the app economy, location services, and mobile-first design.
details.whyItMatters: Smartphones made the internet ubiquitous and always available. More people access the internet by phone than by computer, fundamentally changing how networks are used.
takeaways: The iPhone in 2007 launched the smartphone era
Mobile internet surpassed desktop usage by 2016
Smartphones created the app economy and always-on connectivity

faq.question: How did smartphones change networking requirements?
faq.answer: Smartphones demanded seamless handoffs between cell towers, efficient battery usage for radio connections, and networks that handle billions of small requests. Mobile networks had to evolve from voice-optimized to data-optimized. 4G and 5G were designed primarily for smartphone data.

faq.question: Why did mobile internet become dominant?
faq.answer: Smartphones go everywhere with their owners. For billions of people in developing countries, a phone is their first and only computing device. Always-on connectivity, combined with apps designed for mobile, made phones the primary internet access point for most of humanity.
